title: Atlas Health - Redwood Console Tracing & Debugging Demo
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Console tracing, error analysis, and request logs focused on debugging workflows for Atlas Health's inference pipelines. Demo covered trace navigation, request-level logs, correlating traces to requests, sampling controls, SLO alerting, and next steps to run a short benchmark and share security and pricing docs.
topics: Correlation IDs and KV cache issues
action_items: Jordan Lee - send security whitepaper and SOC2 evidence - due 2027-11-10
Priya Patel - run 1k-request benchmark with Atlas sample prompt set and share results - due 2027-11-12
Maya Chen - provide representative prompt set and production traffic pattern doc - due 2027-11-08
next_steps: Jordan to share pricing and dedicated capacity options
SE to run benchmark on dedicated pool and share latency/cost sheet
Schedule follow-up to review benchmark and pilot scope week of 2027-11-15
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, uh this is Jordan from Redwood, I'll run through the console tracing and debugging flows today. Priya and Samir are here with me.
[00:10] Maya Chen: Hi Jordan, thanks. We are Maya, Liam, Alex, excited to see how tracing maps to errors in prod.
[00:18] Priya Patel: Hey, quick agenda, we'll show trace nav, how to go from an error spike to the single request, look at request logs, and then show some common patterns like KV cache warming, batching issues, and rollout fallbacks.
[00:32] Liam O'Rourke: Sounds good, we mainly want to reduce median latency and find root cause for intermittent 5xxs.
[00:40] Jordan Lee: Great, we'll start. I'll share my screen, give me one sec.
[00:50] [screen share starts] Jordan Lee: Ok on the console home, you'll see per-route latency, token breakdown, and last 24h errors. If you click into Tracing -> Error analysis, you get a waterfall of traces.
[01:10] Priya Patel: One thing to call out, our tracing uses sampling by default but you can increase sampling for routes or by error rate.
[01:25] Jordan Lee: Right, here's an example trace — you can see the model call span, pre-processing, and post-processing. The model call has a long tail so let's click into the request.
[01:38] Maya Chen: I see model-call 2.1s, but why is kv cache showing 800ms?
[01:44] Samir Gomez: Sometimes the transcript picks up KV as "KV cash" in logs, that comes from auto transcription. But the console shows KV cache warms and the cold-start can cost time.
[01:56] Priya Patel: For Atlas, if you have many distinct session prefixes we may not get cache hits — we showed a heatmap earlier in the doc.
[02:08] Alex Rivera: Can we correlate a trace to the raw request payload to see prompt shape?
[02:12] Jordan Lee: Yep, click Request logs -> you get the full request JSON, headers, response and SDK metadata. We redact PII by default, and there's a toggle for full payload if you have the right RBAC.
[02:27] Liam O'Rourke: RBAC and SSO we need — Atlas requires SAML & scoped roles for logs.
[02:33] Jordan Lee: We support SSO/SAML and fine-grained RBAC. I'll attach security docs after the call.
[02:40] [05:00] Priya Patel: Moving on, here's an error analysis dashboard, you can group by model variant, region and hardware type. We often see that custome model variants with quantization produce increased token errors — you'll see the spike if you filter by model quantized.
[05:25] Maya Chen: Do you track per-token CPU/gpu time?
[05:30] Priya Patel: We show token-level latency distribution and break down GPU time vs host pre/post. It's approximate since some kernels overlap but it's useful for regressions.
[06:00] Jordan Lee: Now I'll simulate a 5xx spike — notice the error sample list on the right. Click one, it opens the trace with timeline.
[06:15] [06:30] Jordan Lee: In this example the 5xx is due to OOM on a pinned quantized variant; the trace shows long decode time then a failure at the runtime. The console links to the model variant config and kernel logs.
[06:50] Liam O'Rourke: That level of linkage is helpful. We get errors from our app with a correlation id but it's tedious to chase.
[07:00] Priya Patel: We ingest correlation IDs, request IDs, and you can add your own headers that get indexed. So in the trace you can jump from our request-id to your app logs.
[07:18] Maya Chen: Is there an API to pull traces programmatically for our incident runbook?
[07:24] Jordan Lee: Yep, REST endpoints and SDKs — we'll include a sample script in the repo.
[07:30] [08:00] Samir Gomez: Quick note about sampling: you can set trace retention and also a dynamic sampling rule that increases sampling on error rate thresholds. That helps to not blow up logs costs.
[08:20] Alex Rivera: How long are request logs retained by default?
[08:25] Jordan Lee: Hosted default is 30 days; Dedicated can configure retention and Private deployments can set policy to comply with retention requirements.
[08:35] Liam O'Rourke: For us, 90 days would be ideal for compliance.
[08:40] Jordan Lee: That's possible for Dedicated / Private, we'll detail pricing for extended retention.
[08:50] [10:00] Priya Patel: Now we'll demo a debugging flow: error spike -> open trace -> inspect request payload -> check request logs -> run a repro in the debug runner.
[10:20] Maya Chen: Demo the debug runner please.
[10:25] Priya Patel: Sure, click "Run in Debug" on a request, it opens a sandbox with the same model config and replay of the request. You can toggle quantization and batch size, then re-run to see latency changes.
[10:45] Jordan Lee: This is helpful especially for reproducing differences between hosted and dedicated.
[11:00] Liam O'Rourke: What about network anomalies? Sometimes we see spikes caused by cross-region routing.
[11:10] Priya Patel: Traces include network hops and region tags, so you can filter by region and see if a route had a remote fallback.
[11:25] [12:00] Jordan Lee: Here's another example where a canary rollout caused increased latency — we support rollouts with automatic fallback to stable variant on SLO breaches.
[12:18] Alex Rivera: Can we set automatic fallback thresholds per route?
[12:22] Jordan Lee: Yes, per-route SLOs and policies. We'll show the dashboard later.
[12:30] [13:00] Priya Patel: Now request logs: searching is full text, you can filter by header, response code, and also use a time-series correlation to see requests per minute hitting the model.
[13:20] Maya Chen: Does the search index preserve prompt text? We have PHI so we need redaction.
[13:30] Jordan Lee: By default prompts are redacted in plain text views; Atlas can enable tokenizable prompt storage in dedicated/private with customer-managed keys.
[13:45] Liam O'Rourke: Customer-managed keys (KMS) are a requirement.
[13:50] Jordan Lee: We integrate with AWS KMS and HSM options for Private deployments.
[14:00] [15:00] Samir Gomez: Jumping to error pattern detection — the console flags anomalies and groups similar errors using fuzzy matching; sometimes proper nouns are mis-identified in the transcript, so grouping uses code-level signatures not transcription text.
[15:25] Maya Chen: We also need a way to triage errors by business impact.
[15:30] Priya Patel: You can annotate routes with business tags and we surface business-impacting errors first.
[15:40] [16:00] Jordan Lee: Let's talk about performance tuning — batching and caching levers are exposed in the Optimize tab; you can apply suggestions from our profiler.
[16:18] Liam O'Rourke: If we increase batch size, how do we control tail latency?
[16:22] Priya Patel: You can set latency SLOs and the runtime will trade batch size vs latency; Optimize recommends per-route quantization and batch thresholds based on your request distribution.
[16:40] [18:00] Jordan Lee: Playing with the replay, I'll toggle batch from 8 to 32 — watch the median go down but tail increases, you can see that in the token latency histogram.
[18:20] Maya Chen: Nice. The histogram helps explain why some users see slow responses.
[18:30] [19:00] Priya Patel: Another gotcha — when you pin a model to a region and that region is under maintenance, smart routing can fallback to a compatible variant in another region; traces will show the fallback span.
[19:20] Alex Rivera: Do we get alerted when fallback happens?
[19:25] Jordan Lee: Yes you can alert on fallback rate and on rollout-triggered fallbacks.
[19:40] [21:00] Samir Gomez: Quick show of request-level debugging: opening a failed request, we can see token-level logs, model logits if enabled, and internal runtime metrics.
[21:20] Liam O'Rourke: Log volume could be massive if we enable logits — what's the cost model?
[21:30] Jordan Lee: Logging logits is an opt-in add-on and priced separately; we recommend enabling for short regressions only.
[21:45] Maya Chen: For compliance we need to know who accessed full request logs. Is there audit trail?
[21:50] Priya Patel: Yes, audit logs show user, time, action, and IP. They can be exported to your SIEM.
[22:05] [24:00] Jordan Lee: Now, few questions from the team: Maya asked about KV cache misses earlier — if you see many unique prefixes we can suggest prefix canonicalization or use a small in-memory pre-warm to improve hit rate.
[24:20] Maya Chen: Could you share examples of canonicalization?
[24:25] Priya Patel: Yes, we'll add docs; short answer is normalize user identifiers and strip session-specific metadata before the prefix.
[24:35] [26:00] Alex Rivera: On private deployment, can we keep logs entirely on-prem?
[26:08] Jordan Lee: Yes, Private keeps data in your network and logs can be stored on your infrastructure, KMS keys stay with you.
[26:20] Liam O'Rourke: Good.
[26:30] [28:00] Priya Patel: Let's demo a recent customer case: we found a batch size mismatch across services causing duplicated tokens and increased cost. In the console trace you can see duplicate spans and then the request logs show appended tokens.
[28:20] Maya Chen: How did you detect duplication automatically?
[28:25] Samir Gomez: We use signature matching and token delta heuristics.
[28:35] [30:00] Jordan Lee: We'll run through a quick benchmark now — running 1k requests from our repro harness using Atlas sample prompts.
[30:15] [31:00] Priya Patel: Running... initial results: median 180ms, p95 820ms on hosted variant. When we run the dedicated config with bigger batcher and warmed cache median drops to 120ms and p95 to 420ms.
[31:30] Liam O'Rourke: What's the cost delta roughly?
[31:35] Jordan Lee: Dedicated improves unit cost at scale; we'll send a cost sheet comparing per-1M tokens on hosted vs reserved capacity.
[32:00] [34:00] Maya Chen: Can we test an on-prem variant? We have compliance windows.
[34:15] Priya Patel: For on-prem we'll need to scope the hardware and networking; our solutions team will work with you on firewall/NAT rules and KMS integration.
[34:30] Alex Rivera: Timeline for pilot?
[34:35] Jordan Lee: If we start next week, pilot could be 3-4 weeks including security review and a small dedicated pool.
[34:45] [36:00] Samir Gomez: I'll note an open item to provision a small dedicated cluster for the pilot.
[36:10] Maya Chen: For the benchmark, the sample set we provided earlier is synthetic; we'll send a real traffic slice.
[36:20] Priya Patel: Great, please do. That will help the Optimize recommendations.
[36:30] [38:00] Jordan Lee: Any final technical questions?
[38:10] Liam O'Rourke: One on observability retention — can we stream logs to our Splunk/Datadog?
[38:18] Jordan Lee: Yes, we support log forwarding and webhook sinks; many customers forward audit and request logs to SIEMs.
[38:28] Maya Chen: Also, for SLOs can we tie alerts into PagerDuty?
[38:34] Priya Patel: PagerDuty and Opsgenie are supported, and you can create escalation policies per route.
[38:45] [40:00] Jordan Lee: Recap: we'll run the dedicated benchmark, send security docs, price sheet, and schedule follow-up the week of 2027-11-15.
[40:20] Maya Chen: Sounds good.
[40:30] Alex Rivera: One last ask — can you include an example of a debug runbook for on-call?
[40:36] Jordan Lee: Yes, we'll share a runbook template.
[40:45] [45:00] Samir Gomez: Action items captured in the notes.
[45:10] Priya Patel: I'll follow up on the KV prefix canonicalization examples.
[45:20] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone, we'll send the pack.
[45:30] Maya Chen: Thank you, appreciate the walk-through.
[45:40] [51:30] Jordan Lee: Ok we'll wrap here — thanks all.
[51:40] [screen share ends]
